title: Nothing shall separate (Romans 8:35–39)
hook: neither death nor life nor angels nor height nor depth

segments.voice: Yesterday, sunergei, not the greeting-card version. Your line was all things. What might be woven from a setback? Day five hundred sixty-seven.

Make a list of the things you're most afraid of. Be honest. Losing someone. Getting sick. Being alone. Money running out. Something you did coming to light. Dying. Most of us carry a list like that somewhere below the surface, and it gets louder at night. Paul made one too, at the end of Romans 8. And then he did something unexpected with it. He put the word nothing in front of it.
screen: `A LIST OF YOUR FEARS.` → `PAUL MADE ONE TOO.` → `THEN HE WROTE: NOTHING.`

segments.voice: First, Paul asks the question, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation? or distress? or famine? or nakedness? or danger? or persecution? or the sword?" Those weren't abstractions for Paul. He'd been shipwrecked, beaten with rods, hungry, cold, in danger from rivers and robbers, and tradition says he'd die by the sword in Rome. Then he answers: "But in all these things we overcome, because of him that hath loved us." And then the great list: "For I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor might, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Listen to how he builds it. Mostly in pairs: death and life, angels and principalities, things present and things to come, height and depth. He's covering everything: every moment of time, every corner of space, every power seen and unseen. And just in case he missed something, nor any other creature. Anything that was made. I am sure, he says. Not I hope, not I feel. Convinced. Notice what he doesn't promise. He doesn't say none of these things will happen. Famine and sword might come. He says none of them can cut the thread between you and the love of God. The Church reads this passage at many funerals, because it reaches even past death. And it ends this great chapter that began with no condemnation. From no condemnation to no separation.
screen: `WHO SHALL SEPARATE US?` · `IN ALL THESE THINGS WE OVERCOME.` · `NEITHER DEATH, NOR LIFE, NOR HEIGHT.` · `NOR ANY OTHER CREATURE.` · then, large: `NOTHING SHALL SEPARATE US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your fear, and add nothing separates. Settle, and breathe. Pick one fear from your list. Say it to yourself plainly: losing my job. My diagnosis. My kid's future. Then, after it, in the same breath, add Paul's words: nothing shall separate us. Not as a magic spell that makes the fear go away, but as a sentence put next to it. Do it with a second fear if you like. If you pray, you can rest in the love of God that Paul was sure of. If not, notice what it's like to set a fear beside a promise. The bell holds the time.
Separate. The Greek word behind Paul's great list: nothing in time or space can separate us from the love of God. Today's word.

Your line: nothing shall separate us. Today, when a fear rises, add those words. And that's week eighty-one: justification, poured, buried with him, wretched, the Spirit prays, sunergei, and nothing shall separate. Day five hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Romans 8:31–39 is one of the readings the Church offers for Catholic funeral Masses, and many Catholics keep these verses close in illness and grief.

myth: Paul promises believers that famine and sword won't come
he says they can't separate us from the love of God, not that they won't happen.
Paul had faced many of the dangers on his list
shipwreck, rods, hunger, cold. by tradition he died by the sword in Rome.
Romans 8 begins with no condemnation and ends with no separation
the chapter runs from one to the other.

fork.setup: you're Paul, listing every danger you can think of. what do you do with the list?
options: promise none of it will happen.
say none of it can separate us from God's love.
tell people not to think about it.
fork.reveal: he puts nothing in front of the whole list: neither death, nor life, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us.

original.note: Greek: to separate, divide, put apart. nothing shall be able to separate us.

trapdoor: what you thought: a comforting verse for hard times.
what it means: Paul names every power of time, space and creation, and says none can cut us off from the love of God in Christ.
what a scholar hears: height and depth may echo astrological terms for the heavens, which ancient people feared ruled their fate. Paul places even these under nothing.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of Romans 8:35, 8:37 and 8:38–39 (Douay has 'I am sure' and adds 'nor might').
Romans 8:31b–35, 37–39 in the Order of Christian Funerals readings: confirm.
Paul's death by the sword is tradition, not scripture; the script says so in the myth. Confirm.
Height and depth (hypsōma, bathos) as possible astrological terms: a scholarly suggestion, hedged; confirm.
Week eighty-one counted as days 561–567; confirm the look-back list.
